name: Maneybhanjan
tagline: Border bazaar where the Sandakphu Land Rovers wait
meta_description: Maneybhanjan, the start of the Sandakphu trek: old Land Rovers, the Nepal border culvert, guide office, costs and how to get there from Darjeeling.
summary: Maneybhanjan is the small border town 26 km west of Darjeeling where every Sandakphu trip begins. You hire your compulsory guide and pay park entry here, then either walk up to Chitrey or board one of the town's old Land Rovers. A culvert in the bazaar marks the line with Nepal.

local_story.title: A pass with a prayer wall and a fleet of old jeeps
paras: The name is usually read as Nepali: a bhanjyang is a col or saddle, and mane refers to the mani prayer walls and wheels that Buddhist travellers set up at such crossings. The town sits on that saddle, on the India–Nepal border. The line itself is almost comically modest: a small culvert in the bazaar, which doubles as the motor stand for jeeps to Sukhiapokhri and Darjeeling. Shops on one side take Nepali rupees as easily as Indian ones on the other.

Maneybhanjan's other fame is its Land Rovers. Through the 1950s and 1960s, Series Land Rovers were the only vehicles that could manage the stone track up the Singalila Ridge, and the town kept them long after the rest of India moved on. Today an owners' association runs a fleet of around forty, many more than half a century old, repaired with salvaged parts by local mechanics. They carry trekkers, but also rations, gas cylinders and schoolchildren for the ridge villages.

did_you_know: The India–Nepal border at Maneybhanjan is marked by a small culvert in the bazaar, which also serves as the stand for jeeps to Sukhiapokhri and Darjeeling.
Because the town lies within the Singalila forest area, its growth is restricted to protect the surrounding forest; it has roughly 500 households.
Many Maneybhanjan Land Rovers are Series I and II models from the 1950s and 1960s, kept running for the cobbled 31 km track to Sandakphu.
intro: Most travellers spend an hour in Maneybhanjan, and that is a pity. The bazaar is short and busy in the mornings: porters waiting by the guide office, Land Rover drivers polishing windscreens, women selling oranges and churpi, Nepali shoppers crossing the culvert for Indian goods and Indians crossing back for Nepali ones. Prayer flags run from the gompa above the road, and the first bend of the Sandakphu track leaves right from the end of the street.

It is also the practical heart of the trek. The guide association and park ticketing are here, along with the last proper shops for batteries, snacks, gloves and medicines before the ridge. If you arrive from Darjeeling after 11 am, consider sleeping here and starting fresh; the climb to Chitrey is steep and short days on the ridge begin early. A night in a simple lodge costs far less than a rushed late start.
facts: Land Rovers, guide office, Nepal border
Jio, Airtel and BSNL work in town
costs: Land Rover to Sandakphu and back, one night

highlights.title: The Land Rover stand
highlights.text: A row of green and white Series Land Rovers parks at the head of the Sandakphu track each morning. Drivers will tell you the year of their vehicle with pride. Even if you plan to walk, it is worth a look before the trek, and a ride back down saves sore knees.

highlights.title: The border culvert
highlights.text: Walk to the small culvert in the bazaar and you are standing on the India–Nepal border. There is no gate, only a few shops and the jeep stand. Locals cross freely; trekkers should simply carry ID and not wander further into Nepal than the town.

highlights.title: Guide and park office
highlights.text: The guide association office and the park entry counter are near the start of the trail. You register, pay entry and get a guide assigned in turn from the roster. Arrive by 8–9 am in season to avoid a wait behind larger groups.

highlights.title: Last shopping before the ridge
highlights.text: Pick up batteries, sunscreen, chocolate, dried fruit, gloves and woollen caps in the bazaar. Prices for snacks roughly double by Sandakphu, where everything comes up by Land Rover or on a porter's back, so a small stock here saves real money.

highlights.title: Start of the Chitrey climb
highlights.text: The trail leaves the bazaar and climbs steeply through forest and past chortens to Chitrey, about 3 km and 1.5–2 hours. It is the hardest hour of the first day. Take it slowly; your guide will set a pace that you can keep for a week.

how_to_reach.text: From Darjeeling's Chowk Bazaar motor stand, shared jeeps to Maneybhanjan leave through the morning, about ₹100–150 a seat for ≈ 26 km via Ghoom and Sukhiapokhri, 1–1.5 hours. From Siliguri, take a shared jeep to Mirik or Sukhiapokhri and change. Morning departures are most reliable.

A reserved car from Darjeeling costs about ₹1,500–2,000. From NJP or Bagdogra straight to Maneybhanjan, expect ₹3,500–4,500 and 3.5–4 hours via Mirik or via Ghoom. Leave by 7 am if you plan to walk to Chitrey or Tumling the same day.
Jeeps from Rimbik and Dhotrey come down to Maneybhanjan in the morning on the hill road through Batasey. Ask the night before for times, as there are only a few departures.

where_to_stay: Maneybhanjan has a handful of simple lodges and family hotels along the main road and near the Land Rover stand, with basic rooms for about ₹1,000–1,800 a night and dal-bhat dinners. They are plain but warm, and sleeping here lets you start the trek at 7 am instead of noon. Many trekkers instead stay in Darjeeling and arrive by an early jeep. If you want more comfort, sleep in Darjeeling and book a reserved car for the morning.
tips: Reach the guide office by 8–9 am; in October the queue for guides can take an hour.
Agree the Land Rover fare, return date and waiting charges in writing before you leave.
Buy snacks and a filter bottle here; bottled water on the ridge costs two to three times more.
Carry cash in small notes; there is an ATM in Darjeeling but none on the ridge.
If you arrive after 11 am, stay the night rather than start the steep climb late.

experiences.title: Meet the old Land Rovers at the stand
experiences.summary: Spend half an hour among the Series Land Rovers that have climbed the Singalila Ridge since the 1950s. Talk to drivers, look under a bonnet or two and understand why a town on the Nepal border still runs on British four-wheel drives older than most of their passengers.
body: Mornings at the head of the Sandakphu track are the town's busiest hour. Land Rovers line up in a rough queue, owners checking oil and tyre pressure, porters lashing gas cylinders and rice sacks to the roof racks. Most vehicles are Series I and II models, with flat bonnets, sliding side windows and aluminium bodies that do not rust in the wet ridge air.

The owners run them through an association that fixes the fares and the order of departures, so you take the vehicle whose turn it is rather than choosing by colour. Drivers often know the full history of their Land Rover, who bought it, which engine it now runs and how many times it has been rebuilt. Ask politely; most are happy to talk while they wait.

If you are walking, this is the place to arrange a ride back down from Sandakphu or a lift for your bags. If you are riding, settle the fare, the overnight charge and the return time with the association before you load up. Then climb in at the back, hold the rail and expect four hours of bouncing on the cobbled track.

faqs.q: How old are the Maneybhanjan Land Rovers?
faqs.a: Many are Series I and II Land Rovers built in the 1950s and 1960s, kept running with rebuilt engines and salvaged parts by local mechanics. Each owner maintains his own vehicle within the association's fleet of about forty. You will also see a few newer jeeps on the route, but the old Land Rovers still do most of the work.

faqs.q: How much does a Land Rover to Sandakphu cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively ₹6,500–9,000 for a vehicle to Sandakphu and back with one night's halt, shared by up to six passengers. A one-way drop costs less, and each extra night adds a waiting charge. Rates are fixed by the owners' association and change each season, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do you need a guide if you go by Land Rover?
faqs.a: Yes. The licensed guide rule applies to everyone entering Singalila National Park, including vehicle trips. The guide rides with you, usually in the front, and his daily fee is added to your costs. Arrange the guide and park entry at Maneybhanjan before the Land Rover leaves.

experiences.title: Walk the bazaar on the Nepal border
experiences.summary: A slow walk through Maneybhanjan's one street, from the jeep stand at the border culvert past grocers, momo kitchens and the small gompa, gives you the feel of a frontier town where two countries share one market and one language.
body: Start at the culvert by the motor stand. On one side you are in Darjeeling district, on the other in Nepal's Ilam district, and nobody stops you crossing to buy tea. Nepali shoppers come over for Indian goods; Indian visitors pick up Nepali biscuits and noodles. Prices are shown in Indian rupees on both sides, and Nepali rupees change hands too.

Walk up the street past hardware shops, cloth sellers and the kitchens that steam momos from 8 am. Look for blocks of hard churpi, the dried yak or cow cheese chewed slowly on the trail, and for oranges in winter from the lower valleys. The small gompa above the road, strung with prayer flags, is where many drivers stop to turn the prayer wheels before a long run.

Finish with a cup of milky tea near the Land Rover stand and watch the ridge traffic load up. This is a working town, not a museum, so ask before you photograph people. Do not walk on into Nepal beyond the bazaar without proper papers; for a trekker, the town edge is the sensible limit.

faqs.q: Can you cross into Nepal at Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Locals cross freely within the bazaar, and trekkers routinely step across. Going further into Nepal beyond the town is a different matter: foreigners need a Nepal visa and an official crossing point, and Indians should carry a passport or voter ID. For a trek day, stay within the bazaar. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What should I buy in Maneybhanjan before the trek?
faqs.a: Buy snacks, dried fruit, chocolate, batteries, sunscreen, lip balm, a woollen cap and gloves if you lack them. A block of churpi is a good trail chew. Everything on the ridge comes up by Land Rover or porter, so prices at Sandakphu are roughly double. Carry cash; there are no ATMs on the ridge.

faqs.q: Is Indian currency accepted on the Nepal side?
faqs.a: Yes, along this border Indian rupees are accepted in shops and lodges, including on the Nepal stretches of the trek at Tumling and Jaubari. Small notes are easiest. Nepali shops may give change in Nepali rupees, which are worth less, so carry exact amounts where you can.

experiences.title: Hire your guide and pay park entry
experiences.cost: Guide ₹1,500–2,000 a day per group · entry ≈ ₹100–200
experiences.summary: Every Sandakphu trip starts with paperwork at Maneybhanjan: register with the guide association, get a licensed guide from the roster and buy Singalila National Park entry tickets. Done early, it takes half an hour and sets up the whole trek.
body: The guide association office sits near the start of the trail. Guides are assigned by turn, which spreads work fairly across local families, so you cannot normally pick a person by name unless you have booked through a known operator. Tell the office your route, number of days and whether you will walk or ride; the fee is per group per day and includes the guide's return walk on many routes.

Park entry is paid at the forest counter. Bring photo ID for everyone: passport or voter ID for Indians, passport and Indian visa for foreigners. These are checked again at the park and SSB posts on the ridge, and the trail steps through Nepal more than once. Keep the receipts; you may be asked for them at Tumling or Sandakphu.

Use the time to agree details: where you will sleep each night, whether the guide eats with you (normally you pay for his lodge meals or he arranges his own), and the day you want to come out at Rimbik or back at Maneybhanjan. A clear plan at the office makes the rest of the trek simple.

faqs.q: Can I trek to Sandakphu without a guide?
faqs.a: No. Singalila National Park requires a licensed local guide for every group, and forest staff check at the posts along the ridge. The rule creates income for local families and improves safety in fog and snow. Solo trekkers can share a guide by joining up with others at the office in the morning.

faqs.q: What does a Sandakphu guide cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively ₹1,500–2,000 per group per day, set by the guide association and revised from time to time. You usually also cover the guide's lodge meals or pay a small food allowance. A porter, if you want one, costs extra at about ₹1,000–1,300 a day. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What ID do I need for the Singalila trek?
faqs.a: Indians should carry a passport or voter ID; Aadhaar may not be accepted on the Nepal stretches. Foreigners need a passport with a valid Indian visa. Carry photocopies and the originals, as SSB and forest staff check at several points between Maneybhanjan and Phalut.

experiences.title: Momos and milk tea before the climb
experiences.summary: Fuel up at one of the small kitchens near the jeep stand with a plate of steamed momos, a bowl of thukpa or bread and eggs, and sweet milk tea. It is the cheapest good meal you will eat for days, and the start of the trek's food rhythm.
body: Maneybhanjan's kitchens open early for drivers and porters. Expect plates of six to eight steamed momos filled with pork, chicken or cabbage and served with a fiery tomato and chilli sauce, bowls of thukpa noodle soup, and roti with fried eggs and potato curry. A plate costs roughly ₹70–120 here, about half the ridge price.

Order a glass of milk tea and something with carbohydrate. The first stretch to Chitrey climbs about 400 m in 3 km, and a good breakfast helps. If you are not used to chilli, ask for the sauce on the side; the local version is made with dalle khursani, the small round chilli of these hills, and it is strong.
Pack a few boiled eggs or a roll for the trail; there are tea stops at Chitrey and Meghma, but lunch on the first day is often late. Then pay, pick up your pack and walk to the start of the trail.

faqs.q: What is good to eat in Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Steamed momos, thukpa noodle soup, chowmein and simple roti, egg and potato breakfasts are the standards. Kitchens near the jeep stand open early for drivers. Prices are lower than on the ridge, with a plate of momos around ₹70–120 and tea ₹20–30.

faqs.q: Are there vegetarian options at Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Yes. Most kitchens make vegetable momos with cabbage and onion, vegetable thukpa and dal-bhat. On the ridge, lodge menus are mostly vegetarian anyway, with eggs widely available. Vegans should ask about ghee and butter in dal and roti.

faqs.q: Should I carry food from Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Carry light snacks: dried fruit, nuts, chocolate, biscuits and churpi. Lodges on the ridge serve full meals, so you do not need to carry cooking food. Snacks cost roughly twice as much at Sandakphu, so a small stock bought here saves money and gives energy between lodges.

faqs.q: How far is Maneybhanjan from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 26 km by road via Ghoom and Sukhiapokhri, which takes 1–1.5 hours by shared jeep or car. Shared jeeps leave Darjeeling's Chowk Bazaar motor stand through the morning for about ₹100–150 a seat. A reserved car costs about ₹1,500–2,000. Start early if you want to walk to Tumling the same day.

faqs.q: Can I start the Sandakphu trek on the day I arrive from NJP?
faqs.a: It is possible if you leave NJP or Bagdogra by 6–7 am in a reserved car and reach Maneybhanjan by 10.30 am, then walk to Chitrey or Tumling. By shared jeeps you will arrive too late. Most trekkers spend the first night in Darjeeling or Maneybhanjan and start fresh.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM in Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Do not count on one. Withdraw enough cash in Darjeeling or Siliguri for the whole trek, including guide fees, lodges, food and the Land Rover if you plan one. Card and UPI payments sometimes work in Maneybhanjan, but not reliably on the ridge.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Roughly 2,150 m, though sources vary from about 1,930 m to 2,150 m depending on where in the town it is measured. From here the Sandakphu trail climbs about 1,500 m over three to four days to 3,636 m. The first climb, to Chitrey, gains around 400 m.

faqs.q: Is Maneybhanjan in India or Nepal?
faqs.a: The town is in India's Darjeeling district, but it sits right on the border. A small culvert in the bazaar separates India from Nepal's Ilam district, and a few shops stand on the Nepali side. You can walk across within the bazaar without formalities, but carry ID.

faqs.q: Should I stay overnight in Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Stay if you arrive after about 11 am or want an early start on the trail. A simple lodge room costs about ₹1,000–1,800 and dinner is cheap. If you arrive early by a reserved car, you can walk straight on to Chitrey or Tumling instead.

faqs.q: Can I buy trekking gear in Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Only basics: woollen caps, gloves, socks, raincoats, torches, batteries and snacks. For proper down jackets, sleeping bags or trekking poles, buy or rent in Darjeeling, where several shops near the Mall and Chowk Bazaar rent gear by the day. Some Maneybhanjan guides can arrange rentals too.

faqs.q: Is Maneybhanjan worth visiting without trekking?
faqs.a: For an hour or two, yes, especially if you like old vehicles and border towns. A day trip from Darjeeling combined with a Land Rover ride to Tumling or Tonglu for the view is a good short outing. On its own, the town is small and practical rather than a destination.

faqs.q: What time do jeeps leave Maneybhanjan for Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Shared jeeps to Darjeeling leave from the stand by the border culvert, mostly in the morning and early afternoon, filling before they go. The last reliable departures are mid-afternoon. Ask at the stand the day before, and check current status before you travel.
